The Eastern river Asian pencil halfbeak (Hyporhamphus intermedius) exhibits a maximum recorded fork length of 20.3 centimeters [Li = 20.3 centimeters], a value that positions this species among the larger-bodied members of its genus within Southeast Asian freshwater systems. Field surveys of mature individuals indicate that this asymptotic size is attained after several years of steady somatic growth. At the onset of reproductive maturation, individuals typically measure approximately 10 centimeters [Lp = approximately 10 centimeters] in fork length, a threshold that marks a significant physiological transition. This length at puberty corresponds to a wet body weight of roughly 1.7 grams [Wwp = roughly 1.7 grams], as estimated from length-weight regressions derived from local population samples. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a typical allometric pattern, with the mass at puberty reflecting the accumulation of sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis and spawning. Comparative data from related halfbeak species suggest that this size at maturation is relatively conservative and may be linked to the stable thermal conditions of its lowland riverine habitats.

Reproductive output in Hyporhamphus intermedius is characterized by a relatively low fecundity schedule, with females producing an estimated 150 eggs annually [Ri = 150 eggs annually] when maintained under optimal thermal conditions. This annual fecundity, reported at a water temperature of 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C], is notably modest for a teleost of this body size and reflects a strategy prioritizing egg quality over quantity. Field observations indicate that spawning events are protracted but not continuous, likely involving multiple batches released across several weeks. The relatively low investment in annual reproduction, combined with a high allocation to somatic maintenance, suggests that this species conserves resources for long-term survivorship, perhaps as an adaptation to variable resource availability in its riverine environment. The thermal regime of 20.7 °C appears to be optimal for both gonad maturation and egg development.

Neonatal biology of the Eastern river Asian pencil halfbeak begins with a small yet well-provisioned yolk-sac larva. Upon hatching, the prolarva weighs approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams] wet weight, a mass derived from an egg diameter of approximately 2 millimeters. This minute birth mass reflects a limited endowment of yolk reserves, which the endotrophic larva must absorb over the first few days of exogenous energy independence. The transition to first feeding occurs shortly after the yolk sac is fully resorbed, at which point the mouth gape of the young-of-year has developed sufficiently to capture small zooplankton. The relatively modest investment per offspring, given the low annual fecundity, suggests that each egg receives substantial maternal provisioning in the form of yolk nutrients, likely enhancing larval survival during the critical early feeding phase. This pattern of producing a small number of relatively large eggs is common among freshwater halfbeaks and is thought to improve recruitment success in hydrologically variable environments where early-life mortality can be severe.

Adult Hyporhamphus intermedius attain an asymptotic body mass of around 13.8 grams [Wwi = around 13.8 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species. This ultimate wet weight represents the maximum size reached under natural conditions, as confirmed by repeated sampling of the largest size classes in riverine populations. The mass at puberty, roughly 1.7 grams, thus represents only about 12 percent of the ultimate body mass, indicating that substantial post-maturational growth occurs. This life-history trajectory, typical of many iteroparous teleosts, allows females to achieve greater fecundity at larger body sizes as they age. The modest ultimate mass, combined with the low annual reproduction, positions this species as a slow-growing, late-maturing fish compared to many other freshwater halfbeaks, a pattern that may be linked to the stable but relatively unproductive nature of its riverine habitat.

Longevity has been documented in Hyporhamphus intermedius through mark-recapture studies and otolith analysis, with the oldest individuals reaching an estimated lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years] when maintained under stable thermal conditions of 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C]. This extended lifespan is comparatively long for a fish of its body size and is consistent with a life-history strategy characterized by slow growth, late maturation, and low annual reproductive output. This duration allows multiple spawning seasons over the course of an individual's life, further emphasizing the iteroparous nature of the species. Senescence in this population appears gradual, with older individuals showing a decline in condition factor but continuing to participate in annual spawning events. The relatively long lifespan may confer a demographic advantage in environments where recruitment is sporadic, as it ensures that a reproductive population persists through years of poor juvenile survival. The thermal regime at 20.7 °C seems to facilitate this extended lifespan by maintaining metabolic rates at a moderate level, avoiding the accelerated senescence often seen in tropical fishes under warmer conditions.
